name: Phenibut

lead: Phenibut is a derivative of the neurotransmitter GABA developed in the Soviet Union in the 1960s. It is a prescription drug in Russia and some neighbouring countries for anxiety and insomnia, and is sold online elsewhere as a supplement or 'nootropic'. In looksmaxxing forums it is used to lower social inhibition and boost confidence before going out, so you come across as more sociable.

It acts mainly as an agonist at GABA-B receptors, as baclofen does but with lower affinity, and the R-enantiomer also binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels, as gabapentin does. A phenyl ring lets it cross the blood-brain barrier, unlike plain GABA. Published human evidence is limited, largely Soviet-era work, animal studies and case reports.

paras: Users take it occasionally before social events to feel looser and more talkative. Effects are felt within hours, and communities discuss spacing out use because tolerance builds.

Reported effects include sedation, nausea, dizziness and next-day hangover. Tolerance builds quickly, and case reports describe withdrawal with rebound anxiety, insomnia, hallucinations, seizures and psychosis. It potentiates alcohol, opioids and other depressants. In the US the FDA determined in 2023 that it is not a lawful dietary ingredient, and several countries have banned or scheduled it.

angle.text: Forum users take phenibut as a 'low inhib' drug for social ease, expecting more confidence and better reactions from others. Its tranquilizer effects are documented, as are tolerance and withdrawal; published human trial data are scarce.

lead: Phenibut (beta-phenyl-gamma-aminobutyric acid) is a central nervous system depressant structurally related to the neurotransmitter GABA. It was developed in the Soviet Union and entered clinical use in Russia in the 1960s as a tranquilizer with cognition-enhancing ('nootropic') properties [1][2][3]. A phenyl ring added to the GABA backbone lets it cross the blood-brain barrier, which plain GABA does poorly [1].

For looks, the appeal described by users is social rather than structural: people take it to lower inhibition and anxiety so they can come across as more confident, talkative and approachable, and to feel at ease in photos, dates and nights out. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed chiefly as a 'low inhib' aid for social situations, often next to alcohol, gabapentinoids and benzodiazepines [4][5]. The chain proponents describe is: less social anxiety, then more relaxed body language and eye contact, then better social reception.

It remains a prescription medicine in Russia and some neighbouring countries for anxiety, insomnia and other conditions, while elsewhere it is sold online as a supplement and is used non-medically for anxiety reduction and euphoria [1][3][6]. Published human evidence consists largely of Soviet-era clinical work, animal pharmacology and, more recently, case series of toxicity and withdrawal; several 2023-2024 reviews collect these [2][7][8][9][10]. Regulators have moved against it in a number of countries, including the United States, Australia, France, Italy and Hungary [1].

paras: In Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Georgia and Latvia, phenibut is approved for anxiety, insomnia and a range of other indications including asthenia, alcohol withdrawal, post-traumatic stress and motion sickness, per Wikipedia's summary of prescribing information [1]. A 2001 review described it as a tranquilizer and nootropic introduced into clinical practice in Russia in the 1960s [2]. It was included in Soviet spacecraft medical kits from 1975 [1].

The licensed drug is made as tablets and as a solution for infusion, and Wikipedia's summary of Russian prescribing information lists indications that include stuttering, tics, vestibular disorders, Meniere's disease and motion sickness alongside anxiety and sleep problems [1]. A Russian randomised crossover study compared two phenibut-type products for bioequivalence in 18 healthy volunteers [11], and a 1998 trial examined phenibut and a beta-blocker, alone and combined, on the functional state of people exposed to heat [12].

Outside licensed countries it is sold online as a supplement, often for self-medication of social anxiety, and users seek anxiolysis, sociability and euphoria [1][6]. A 2016 survey-based review documented online availability, patterns of use, desired effects and acute toxicity [6]. Its appearance relevance is indirect: forum users describe it as a way to appear more confident or approachable.

In forums the effect is described as a short window of social ease, sometimes compared to the feel of alcohol or a benzodiazepine without the same intoxication. Posters in one popular thread describe it as removing most of their anxiety and giving a confidence and motivation lift, while also reporting nausea afterwards and noting how quickly tolerance limits repeat use [4]. Some posters link this to their goals of dating or interviewing more comfortably; others in the same communities describe the effect as disinhibition similar to alcohol [5].

Phenibut was synthesised at the Herzen Leningrad Pedagogical Institute by the group of Professor Vsevolod Perekalin and tested at the Institute of Experimental Medicine of the USSR Academy of Medical Sciences, entering clinical use in Russia in the 1960s [1][2]. Early names included fenigam, and the drug is sold under names such as Noofen, Anvifen, Fenibut and Bifren [1].

Wikipedia reports that from 1975 phenibut was part of Soviet spacecraft medical kits, described as a means of normalising neuropsychological state and improving sleep, with crew medication records linking it to the Salyut 4, 5 and 6 missions [1]. The CNS Drug Reviews article of 2001 introduced the drug to Western readers as a tranquilizer and nootropic [2].

From roughly the 2010s, English-language users began buying it online as a supplement. A 2016 study of availability and use documented the online market and its acute toxicity [6], and a 2024 review notes that it has made inroads into European and US markets marketed for purported nootropic properties [7].

Phenibut is primarily a GABA-B receptor agonist with some GABA-A activity [2]. Its affinity at GABA-B is far lower than baclofen's, and the R-enantiomer is the active form [3][13]. R-phenibut also binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-dependent calcium channels and showed gabapentin-like antinociceptive effects in animal tests [14]. Soviet-era studies reported dopaminergic effects, but the mechanism is described as unclear [1][2].

Wikipedia reports that phenibut acts as a GABA-B full agonist with roughly 30- to 68-fold lower affinity than baclofen in rat-brain assays, and that the (R)-enantiomer has more than 100-fold higher GABA-B affinity than the (S)-form; both enantiomers bind the alpha-2-delta calcium-channel subunit with micromolar affinity [1]. The 2008 comparison of optical isomers found the pharmacological activity of the racemate attributable mainly to the (R)-form [13]. A 2024 review describes additional activity at GABA-A and beta-phenethylamine receptors [7].

Wikipedia reports oral bioavailability of at least 63% at a 250 mg dose and an elimination half-life of about 5.3 hours, with most excreted unchanged in urine, and notes that published human pharmacokinetic data are sparse [1].
Wikipedia notes that only a small share of an oral dose is reported to reach the brain and that a large portion is excreted unchanged in urine [1].

Phenibut is a synthetic aromatic amino acid with the formula C10H13NO2, a GABA analogue with a phenyl ring at the beta position; it is closely related to baclofen (which carries a chlorine on the ring) and to pregabalin [1]. It is chiral, and medicines contain the racemic mixture [1][13].

Reported effects include sedation, nausea, irritability, dizziness, headache and, at high doses, incoordination and next-day hangover [1]. Overdose case descriptions include severe drowsiness, vomiting, low blood pressure and fatty liver changes, with no specific antidote; treatment is supportive [1][6]. Phenibut can potentiate alcohol, opioids and other sedatives [1].

A systematic review of 62 published cases of phenibut toxicity or withdrawal (36 studies) found that about 81% of patients were male, average age about 31, and that around 87% obtained the substance online; roughly 63% had also used other substances, most often benzodiazepines and alcohol [10]. The most common features of toxicity were altered mental status, somnolence, psychosis and movement disorders, and nearly half of the toxicity cases in that review required intubation; average hospital stays were about five days for toxicity and nearly eight for withdrawal [10]. A 2024 toxicology review concluded that some reported effects are life-threatening, that supportive care is complicated by limited pharmacological knowledge, and that co-ingestion of other substances is frequent [7]. Individual overdose reports are also published [15].
Wikipedia cites a 2020 CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report describing three deaths associated with phenibut, only one of which involved phenibut alone [1].

Tolerance develops readily with repeated use. A 2019 literature review and case report described acute withdrawal featuring rebound anxiety, insomnia, agitation, hallucinations and seizures, and baclofen has been used in managing phenibut dependence [1][16]. Contraindications listed for the licensed drug include pregnancy, breastfeeding, liver failure and young age [1].

A 2024 systematic review of 15 withdrawal case reports found an average patient age near 32, mostly men, with a majority presenting to emergency departments and a history of alcohol or other drug use in about three-quarters [8]. A pharmacology review of 29 withdrawal cases reported that patients were treated successfully with baclofen, benzodiazepines or phenobarbital, alone or combined, and noted there are no comparative trials of these approaches [9]. Single case reports of dependence were published as early as 2013 [17], and a primary-care case review addresses dependence and withdrawal [18].
Pregnancy, breastfeeding, liver failure and gastrointestinal ulcerative lesions are listed for the licensed drug, and it is advised not to be combined with alcohol [1].

Controlled modern human trials for anxiety or social confidence are largely absent from the literature. A 2001 review summarised mostly Russian-language clinical and preclinical work and noted anxiolytic and nootropic effects with comparisons to other tranquilizers [2]. Pharmacology studies in animals compared the isomers [13] and examined calcium-channel binding [14]. A 2016 study characterised use, desired effects and toxicity in non-medical users rather than testing efficacy [6]. A 2019 review collected withdrawal case reports [16].

More recent literature is mainly descriptive. A 2022 study measured the quantity of phenibut in dietary supplements before and after FDA warnings [19]; Wikipedia reports that US products labelled as containing phenibut have been found to hold anywhere from none to over 1,100 mg per serving [1]. Systematic reviews of toxicity and withdrawal cases, rather than efficacy trials, form the bulk of the 2023-2024 evidence [8][9][10].

In the US phenibut is an unapproved drug. The FDA determined in 2023 that it is not a lawful dietary ingredient, which makes supplements containing it misbranded; the agency had issued warning letters in 2019 [1][19]. Alabama placed it in Schedule II in November 2021 [1].

Internationally, Australia placed it in Schedule 9 (prohibited) in February 2018 after the Therapeutic Goods Administration cited withdrawal and overdose risks, Hungary added it to its new-psychoactive-substances list on 14 November 2018, Italy on 26 August 2020, and France added it to its controlled list on 18 September 2020; Germany controls it under its NpSG law and Lithuania lists it. Canada and the UN have not scheduled it, and in Russia it is prescription-only [1].

On looksmax.org, users describe phenibut as a way to feel less inhibited and more confident when socialising [4][5]. Posters report both enthusiastic anecdotes and gastrointestinal side effects, and note that tolerance builds quickly [4]. Others in the same threads attribute the perceived social benefit to placebo or to alcohol-like disinhibition [5]. Community members also discuss obtaining it across borders and combining it with other substances, which the research literature identifies as a risk factor [1][6].
Drug-safety reviews observe that online marketing is difficult to control and recommend adding phenibut to drug-screening tests and developing agreed treatment approaches for withdrawal [7][9].
